newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Egyptian cleric urges Afghans to stop fighting.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian cleric urges Afghans to stop fighting.

text.p: The head of one of the world's leading Islamic institutions called on Afghans on Friday to halt their fratricidal war and live together in peace.

"We ask you, we appeal to you, brothers and sons, to lay down your weapons and to live all together as loving brothers," Mohammed Sayed Tantawi, Grand Sheikh of Cairo's al-Azhar University, said during a visit to Islamabad.

Tantawi, delivering a Friday sermon at the city's Faisal Mosque, was quoted by Pakistan's official APP news agency as reminding Afghans of a Koranic verse saying that "he who kills a believer by design shall burn in hell fire for ever".
He urged Afghans to negotiate, saying they had earned the world's respect when they cleared their Soviet-occupied land of "communism and heinous imperialism" in the 1980s.
"Today the whole world is watching you killing each other and you are still Moslems," Tantawi said. "Everyone is wondering and astonished at what is happening amongst you."
The Egyptian cleric did not refer directly to the radical Islamist Taleban now ruling Kabul or any other of the Afghan factions that have fought relentlessly for power.

The Taleban, a Sunni Moslem group, have tried to impose a harsh interpretation of Islamic Sharia law on Afghanistan, effectively banning most women from working or learning and forcing them to veil themselves from head to foot in public.
Tantawi, in what could be taken as criticism of Taleban strictures, advocated "educating yourself and spreading useful knowledge amongst men and women alike, children and adults".

The Taleban, recruited from religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan, burst on to the Afghan scene two years ago, vowing to sweep away "corrupt" mujahideen guerrilla factions and introduce a purist new Islamic order throughout the country.
The militant black-bearded warriors captured Kabul and ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani on September 27.
But they are now locked in bruising battles north of Kabul with the forces of Rabbani's military chief, Ahmad Shah Masood, newly allied with those of Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum.
